# Assumptions Belong to Claims

For independent experimental units, a linear model starts with a conditional
mean:

$$
Y_i=\mathbf{x}_i^\mathsf{T}\boldsymbol\beta+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad
\operatorname{E}(\varepsilon_i\mid\mathbf X)=0.
$$

Different conclusions require different assumptions. Ordinary least squares
(OLS) can always compute the best-fitting linear projection when the design
matrix has full column rank. Interpreting its coefficients as a correctly
specified conditional mean additionally requires the mean model to be adequate.
Classical standard errors require the variance and dependence model; exact
small-sample $t$ and $F$ inference adds conditional normality. Causal
interpretation needs design assumptions that residual plots cannot establish.

| Goal | Central requirements |
|---|---|
| Compute a unique OLS fit | Full column rank and more observations than fitted coefficients |
| Estimate the stated conditional-mean coefficients without bias | $\operatorname{E}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid\mathbf X)=\mathbf 0$ |
| Use the classical covariance formula | Constant conditional variance and uncorrelated errors |
| Use exact small-sample $t$ and $F$ laws | Conditional Gaussian errors in addition to the classical conditions |
| Generalize to a target population | A defensible sampling frame and stable data-generating process |
| Interpret a coefficient causally | Exchangeability or randomization, positivity, consistency, and an appropriate adjustment set |

The experimental unit is the unit whose error contributes independent
information. Replicate reads, wells, images, or cells nested within the same
specimen are not automatically independent experimental units.

# The Assumptions, One by One

## Linear conditional mean

The model asserts

$$
\operatorname{E}(Y_i\mid\mathbf x_i)
=\mathbf x_i^\mathsf{T}\boldsymbol\beta.
$$

"Linear" means linear in $\boldsymbol\beta$; predictors may enter through
polynomials, splines, indicators, or interactions. A curved residual trend can
indicate a missing transformation or nonlinear term. A group-specific trend can
indicate a missing interaction. If the mean is misspecified, an OLS coefficient
usually estimates a design-dependent linear projection rather than the intended
scientific contrast.

## Zero conditional mean

The condition

$$
\operatorname{E}(\varepsilon_i\mid\mathbf X)=0
$$

rules out systematic residual association with the included design. It can fail
because of omitted causes, selection, reverse causation, measurement error, or a
wrong mean function. Residuals are algebraically orthogonal to fitted design
columns, so a residual plot against an included predictor cannot prove this
population condition. Study design, subject-matter knowledge, negative controls,
and sensitivity analysis are essential.

## Variance and dependence

The classical model uses

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid\mathbf X)
=\sigma^2\mathbf I.
$$

Its two parts are distinct:

- **Homoskedasticity:** every unit has the same conditional error variance.
- **No residual dependence:** off-diagonal conditional covariances are zero.

Heteroskedasticity does not by itself bias OLS coefficients under a correct mean
model, but it invalidates the usual covariance estimator and makes OLS
inefficient. Correlation within people, plates, families, time series, or spatial
regions requires a cluster-aware, longitudinal, spatial, mixed, or generalized
least-squares analysis. A heteroskedasticity-consistent standard error does not
repair dependence.

## Rank, overlap, and extrapolation

With $k$ fitted coefficients, $\mathbf X$ must have rank $k$ for a unique
coefficient vector. Near collinearity can leave fitted values stable while making
individual coefficients highly variable. Even with full rank, a conditional
contrast may depend on sparse combinations of covariates. Diagnostics should
therefore examine predictor distributions, cross-tabulations, condition numbers,
and the range over which predictions are requested—not only residuals.

## Conditional normality

Gaussian errors are not needed to define OLS or to make it unbiased under the
mean model. They yield exact finite-sample reference distributions:

$$
\frac{\hat\beta_j-\beta_j}{\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\beta_j)}
\sim t_{n-k}.
$$

Without normality, large-sample inference may still work under suitable moment,
leverage, and independence conditions. Severe skewness, heavy tails, sparse
groups, or a few dominant observations can make that approximation inaccurate.

# Residuals and Leverage

Let

$$
\mathbf H=\mathbf X(\mathbf X^\mathsf{T}\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\mathsf{T},
\qquad
\mathbf e=(\mathbf I-\mathbf H)\mathbf Y.
$$

The diagonal $h_{ii}$ is the leverage of unit $i$. It depends only on the design
matrix and measures how unusual the predictor configuration is relative to the
others. Because $\sum_i h_{ii}=k$, average leverage is $k/n$.

Raw residual variances are unequal even under the homoskedastic model:

$$
\operatorname{Var}(e_i\mid\mathbf X)=\sigma^2(1-h_{ii}).
$$

An internally studentized residual is therefore

$$
r_i=\frac{e_i}{s\sqrt{1-h_{ii}}}.
$$

Externally studentized residuals replace $s$ with an estimate computed after
deleting unit $i$, making them more useful for judging an unusual response. A
large residual means poor vertical fit; high leverage means an unusual predictor
pattern. Influence requires the combination: an observation far out in predictor
space can materially move the fit when its response disagrees with the trend.

Cook's distance summarizes the change in all fitted values after deleting unit
$i$:

$$
D_i=
\frac{e_i^2}{k s^2}
\frac{h_{ii}}{(1-h_{ii})^2}.
$$

There is no universal cutoff that turns an observation into an error. Leverage,
studentized residuals, Cook's distance, DFBETAs, and deletion fits are prompts for
record verification and sensitivity analysis, not automatic deletion rules.

# A Diagnostic Sequence

Diagnostics work best as a structured comparison between observed data and the
model's implications.

1. **Verify design and units.** Confirm randomization, nesting, repeated measures,
   batches, missingness, coding, and which units are independent.
2. **Inspect predictors before fitting.** Check ranges, sparse categories,
   impossible combinations, overlap, rank, and potential extrapolation.
3. **Check the mean structure.** Plot residuals against fitted values, continuous
   predictors, time or order, and scientifically important groups. Add a smooth
   trend as a diagnostic, not as proof of a replacement model.
4. **Check conditional spread.** Look for funnels, group-specific variance, and
   variance related to expected measurement scale.
5. **Check distributional shape when it matters.** A normal quantile--quantile
   plot is relevant to exact small-sample inference and tail behavior, not to the
   existence of the OLS estimate.
6. **Assess influence.** Examine leverage, externally studentized residuals,
   Cook's distance, and coefficient changes under justified deletion checks.
7. **Refit scientifically plausible alternatives.** Compare transformations,
   curvature, interactions, variance models, cluster-aware uncertainty, and
   robust procedures.
8. **Validate the intended use.** For prediction, assess held-out calibration and
   error. For explanation, check whether the coefficient still answers the
   prespecified estimand.

Formal tests of normality or heteroskedasticity can supplement this workflow, but
they do not replace plots and design reasoning. With small $n$, they have little
power; with very large $n$, they can flag negligible deviations. Repeatedly
changing a model until every diagnostic test is nonsignificant also makes the
reported inference conditional on an unreported selection process.

# Reading Common Diagnostic Displays

| Display or quantity | Pattern worth investigating | Possible mechanisms | Appropriate response |
|---|---|---|---|
| Residuals versus fitted values | Curvature | Nonlinear mean, omitted interaction, wrong link | Add justified structure; compare partial effects and predictions |
| Scale--location plot | Increasing or group-specific spread | Heteroskedasticity, scale-dependent measurement | Transform, model variance, or use valid robust covariance |
| Normal Q--Q plot | Strong tail departures or asymmetry | Heavy tails, mixture, coding error, wrong outcome model | Verify records; use robust or outcome-appropriate model; simulate finite-sample behavior |
| Residuals versus order, time, or batch | Runs or shifts | Drift, autocorrelation, unmodeled batch | Include design factors or use dependence-aware model |
| Leverage and Cook's distance | A few dominant units | Sparse design, extreme predictor values, unusual outcomes | Verify and report deletion or perturbation sensitivity |
| Component-plus-residual plot | Predictor-specific curvature | Missing transformation or nonlinear partial effect | Use a prespecified transformation or flexible smooth |

The same visual pattern can have several causes. A funnel may reflect true
heteroskedasticity, an inappropriate response scale, or a mean--variance relation
requiring a generalized linear model. Diagnostics localize tension; they do not
identify a unique repair.

# Worked Bioinformatics Example

Suppose normalized gene expression is measured for 48 independent patient
specimens, with treatment, age, and sequencing batch as predictors. Each specimen
was sequenced in two lanes and lane counts were combined before analysis.

- The 48 patients—not the 96 lanes or millions of reads—are the experimental
  units for treatment inference.
- A residual shift by batch suggests incomplete technical adjustment or an
  interaction, while a residual trend with fitted expression suggests mean or
  variance misspecification.
- One high-leverage patient may combine an age and treatment pattern scarcely
  represented elsewhere. Its influence reveals weak support for that conditional
  comparison; deletion cannot create the missing overlap.
- If residual variance increases with mean expression, robust standard errors may
  protect coefficient inference asymptotically, but a count model or mean--variance
  model may better represent the measurement process.

Statistically, diagnostics ask whether the coefficient and its uncertainty are
stable under credible alternatives. Biologically, they do not establish that a
gene-expression association is causal, functionally important, or transferable
to another tissue or population.

# What Diagnostics Cannot Prove

Residual checks use observed variables and the fitted sample. They cannot prove:

- absence of unmeasured confounding or selection bias;
- independence when the sampling hierarchy was discarded;
- correct measurement of the response and predictors;
- validity outside the observed predictor range or target population;
- biological importance of a statistically precise coefficient.

A satisfactory residual plot means only that the chosen diagnostic did not expose
that kind of discrepancy at its available resolution. It is not a certificate
that the model is true.

# Connections and Take-home Messages

- [Multiple linear regression](multiple-linear-regression.qmd) defines the
  conditional-mean model and coefficient comparisons being diagnosed.
- [Least squares and the geometry of regression](least-squares-and-regression-geometry.qmd)
  derives projection, residual orthogonality, leverage, and rank.
- [Regression uncertainty and coefficient interpretation](regression-uncertainty-and-coefficient-interpretation.qmd)
  separates coefficient, contrast, mean-response, and prediction uncertainty.
- [Robust standard errors and robust regression](robust-standard-errors-and-robust-regression.qmd)
  distinguishes covariance protection from resistance to influential outcomes.
- [Sensitivity analysis and robustness](../statistical-inference/sensitivity-analysis-and-robustness.qmd)
  organizes conclusions across plausible assumptions and analysis choices.

1. State the inferential goal before deciding which assumptions matter.
2. Residuals diagnose the fitted mean and error structure but cannot establish
   exogeneity, causality, or correct replication.
3. Heteroskedasticity, dependence, nonlinearity, and influence are different
   problems and require different responses.
4. Investigate influential observations transparently; never delete them solely
   because a generic threshold was crossed.
5. In bioinformatics, preserving the biological experimental unit is more
   important than the nominal number of technical measurements.
